## A sentence {.activity}

\

> I swim Tuesday and Thursday and either Saturday or Sunday.

\

**What is the fewest number of swims consistent with what I said?**

\_\_\_\_\_\_

{{< countdown minutes=2 >}}

::: notes
Collect answers before advancing. Expect 3 and 4. Push for anyone who says 1.
Do not resolve it yet.
:::

## Three readings

| Reading | Fewest swims |
|---|:---:|
| $\text{Tue} \wedge \text{Thu} \wedge (\text{Sat} \vee \text{Sun})$ | 3 |
| $\text{Tue} \wedge \text{Thu} \wedge (\text{Sat} \oplus \text{Sun})$ | 3 |
| $(\text{Tue} \wedge \text{Thu} \wedge \text{Sat}) \vee \text{Sun}$ | 1 |

\

Same words. Three answers.

::: notes
Reading 2: "either/or" in English often excludes. Reading 3: drop the
parentheses and apply the usual precedence, $\wedge$ before $\vee$. A lone
Sunday swim satisfies it.
:::

## Where the third reading comes from

$$\text{Tue} \wedge \text{Thu} \wedge \text{Sat} \vee \text{Sun}$$

\

$\wedge$ binds tighter than $\vee$, so this groups as

$$(\text{Tue} \wedge \text{Thu} \wedge \text{Sat}) \vee \text{Sun}$$

\

Set $\text{Sun} = $ T and the rest F. Is the sentence satisfied? \_\_\_\_\_\_

How many swims? \_\_\_\_\_\_

## What about Monday? {.activity}

The sentence says nothing about Monday, Wednesday, Friday.

\

Model the week as 7 Boolean variables. Under reading 1, how many *weeks*
satisfy the sentence?

\

Tue, Thu forced: \_\_\_\_\_\_ ways

Sat/Sun: \_\_\_\_\_\_ ways

Mon, Wed, Fri: \_\_\_\_\_\_ ways

Total: \_\_\_\_\_\_

{{< countdown minutes=4 >}}

::: notes
$1 \times 3 \times 2^3 = 24$. Under reading 2, $1 \times 2 \times 8 = 16$.

Two different counting questions: how many swims, versus how many worlds.
The unconstrained variables are easy to miss.
:::

## The fix

To say which reading you mean, you need a notation where the grouping cannot
be dropped.

\

We will build one.

## WFFs

A _well-formed formula_ is a Boolean statement generated by these rules:

```{bnf}
<wff> ::= <atom>
        | ~ <wff>
        | ( <wff> ∧ <wff> )
        | ( <wff> ∨ <wff> )

<atom> ::= p | q | r | s | ...
```

This is a _Grammar_.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_: `<wff>` and `<atom>`

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_: `p`, `q`, `r`, `s` ...

Our first _recursive_ definition.

## Derivation

```{bnf}
<wff> ::= <atom>
        | ~ <wff>
        | ( <wff> ∧ <wff> )
        | ( <wff> ∨ <wff> )

<atom> ::= p | q
```

Example derivation:

`<wff>`

## Notes

*   Every $\wedge$ and $\vee$ arrives with its own parentheses. Reading 3 is
    not expressible.

*   Grammars construct many other kinds of sequences.

*   We could have added $\rightarrow$, $\leftrightarrow$, $\oplus$, $\uparrow$.

*   Evaluating a `<wff>` computationally is DSCI 221. Here we trust Python.

*   The `<wff>` are _propositions_.

## WFF Puzzle {.activity}

Which of these are WFFs?

```{bnf}
<wff> ::= <atom>
        | ~ <wff>
        | ( <wff> ∧ <wff> )
        | ( <wff> ∨ <wff> )

<atom> ::= p | q
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
1.  $(\neg p ∧ (q ∨ r))$
2.  $((p ∧ q) ∨ (r ∧ \neg s))$
3.  $((\neg p) ∨ (q ∨ r))$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
4.  $(p ∨ (qr))$
5.  $\neg (p ∨ (q ∧ \neg r))$
6.  $\neg (p ∨ q))$
:::
:::::

{{< countdown minutes=3 >}}

::: notes
Symbols vary between sources: $pq$, $p \wedge q$, `p & q`, `p && q`. Our grammar
uses one. Be agile.
:::

## A theorem

```{bnf}
<wff> ::= <atom>
        | ~ <wff>
        | ( <wff> ∧ <wff> )
        | ( <wff> ∨ <wff> )

<atom> ::= p | q
```

**Theorem:** $\neg (p ∨ q))$ is not a WFF.

Proof:

::: notes
Suppose it is. Then `~ <wff>` was the last rule applied, so $(p ∨ q))$ is a
`<wff>`. Then `( <wff> ∨ <wff> )` was last, so $p$ and $q)$ are `<wff>`. But
$q)$ matches no rule. So it both is and is not a `<wff>`.

Ask: where have we done this before? Sages and Tricksters, lecture 1. Assume a
role, derive a contradiction, discard the assumption. Same move.
:::

## Same move as Monday

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Sages & Tricksters**

Assume Priya is a Sage.

Then her answers must agree.

They do not.

So she is not a Sage.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The theorem**

Assume $\neg (p ∨ q))$ is a WFF.

Then $q)$ must be a WFF.

No rule produces it.

So it is not a WFF.
:::
:::::

\

This strategy has a name: _proof by contradiction_.

## Propositions

A _proposition_ is a statement that is either **True** or **False**.

*   $37 > 12$

*   Fewer than 5 people in this room feel sleepy.

*   There are extra-terrestrial life forms.

*   This statement is False.

*   $\underline{\hspace{10em}}$

::: notes
Fourth is not a proposition. Third is, and we cannot evaluate it --- being a
proposition does not require knowing the value.
:::

## Translation {.activity}

From English to logic and back.

\

$p$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ate cereal for breakfast.

$q$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ brought a backpack to class.

\

*   $(p\lor q)$

*   $(p\wedge q)$

*   $\neg q$

*   Now the swim sentence: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
